candidates.exact_span: The following Minimum Quantification Levels (MQL's) are to be used for reporting pollutant data for NPDES permit applications and/or compliance reporting.
candidates.computation_change_reason: Whether this appendix governs only application reporting or also FY2025 compliance reporting is ambiguous ('and/or'). If MQLs are treated as operative for compliance reporting, they can change how reported values are interpreted for limit comparisons (A), whether listed pollutants must be reported when monitored (B), and how sub-MQL or non-quantified results are classified (C). If treated as non-operative for compliance, those computations would differ.

The table specifies µg/l as the unit for all listed MQL values. A different unit interpretation (e.g., mg/L) would rescale every numeric MQL and any derived compliance comparison that depends on quantification level relative to an enforceable limit stated in another unit.

Mercury is assigned two different MQL values with a footnote marker but no explanatory footnote text in this segment. Selecting 0.0005 versus 0.005 changes the quantification threshold used when interpreting mercury measurements, which can change whether a result is treated as quantified for limit comparison (A) and whether a reported value is classified as adequate evidence, a documented no-data/below-quantification state, or unresolved missing evidence (C).

Total cyanide and weak-acid-dissociable cyanide are distinct parameters with separate MQL entries. Interpreting which row applies to a given reported cyanide measurement changes the applicable quantification level and therefore whether the result can be compared to an enforceable cyanide limit (A) and how sub-MQL or parameter-mismatched results are categorized (C).

This entry assigns an MQL specifically to total residual chlorine. If a measurement is reported for a related but differently named chlorine parameter, whether this 33 µg/l MQL applies changes quantification treatment for limit comparison (A) and whether the evidence is treated as a valid numeric result versus a missing or below-quantification case (C).

The dioxin congener has an extremely low MQL. Interpreting whether this MQL governs reported dioxin/TCDD results affects whether near-limit or non-detect values are treated as quantified for compliance comparison (A) and whether absent or below-MQL dioxin data is documented no-data versus unresolved missing evidence (C).

The pollutant name is misspelled ('Thalllium' versus thallium). Matching this row to reported thallium data is ambiguous; applying or failing to apply this 0.5 µg/l MQL changes quantification-based limit comparison (A) and missing-evidence classification for thallium results (C).
